title: Multivariate Distributional Reinforcement Learning Using Sliced Divergences
claim: Our evaluation uses a simple chain environment whose vector-valued positional rewards make multivariate return distributions easy to interpret.
layout: 1 panel, left-to-right chain of state circles, curved reset arcs above
description: A single-row state diagram of a chain MDP. Four large empty circles labeled S0, S1, S_{k-2} and S_{k-1} sit along the bottom, joined by straight left-to-right arrows. An ellipsis between S1 and S_{k-2} stands for the omitted middle states. Two curved arrows return to S0, one from S1 (a short arc) and one from S_{k-2} (a long arc spanning the figure), showing the reset transitions. Each transition has a vector reward label in gray text, such as r = [0 1 … 0] on the first forward step and r = [1 0 … 0] on the resets. The labels are one-hot vectors that mark the entered state. The figure is monochrome gray on white. The eye goes first to the long arc and the circles. The sparse layout keeps attention on the reward vectors.
caption: Chain policy-evaluation MDP: states $s_0\!\to\! s_{K-1}$ (terminal). From any nonterminal $s_i$, action fwd moves to $s_{i+1}$ with probability\ 0.9 and resets to $s_0$ with probability\ 0.1; bwd swaps these probabilities. Positional-reward variant: $R_{t+1}=e_{S_{t+1}}\in\mathbb{R}^K$ (one-hot of the entered state).
abstract: Distributional reinforcement learning (DRL) models the full return distribution rather than expectations, but extending it to multivariate settings remains challenging. Many common metrics do not naturally generalize beyond one dimension or lose computational tractability, and the multivariate case introduces additional difficulties such as general matrix discounting, for which no contraction results are available. We introduce Sliced Distributional Reinforcement Learning (SDRL), which lifts tractable one-dimensional divergences to multivariate return distributions via projections. We prove Bellman contraction for uniform slicing under shared scalar discounting, and introduce a maximum-slicing variant with contraction under general dense discount matrices. SDRL supports a broad class of base divergences; we analyze Wasserstein, CramÃ©r, and Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD), and characterize which SDRL variants suit the standard single-sample Bellman update used in distributional RL. We evaluate SDRL on a toy chain problem and a gridworld image-based environment as well as a subset of Atari games.
